{"content": "3658|# Chapter 35: The Memorial
3659|
3660|![](chapter_images/ch35.png)
3661|
3662|The shadow of Proxima b's eastern ridge crept across the memorial site as the red dwarf sun tracked its slow arc overhead. Maya Volkov stood at the edge of the excavated plaza, watching her construction team position the final support columns — each one cast from salvaged hull sections of the *Santiago*.
3663|
3664|Three hundred and ten names. Three hundred and ten reasons why her hands wouldn't stop shaking.
3665|
3666|"Structural integrity verified," Kenji reported through her earpiece. "Ready for the capstone."
3667|
3668|Maya studied the crane's positioning. The massive triangular structure would cap the memorial's apex at precisely thirty-seven degrees — matching the angle of the *Santiago's* fatal approach vector. The numbers lived in her head now, unwanted permanent residents. Thirty-seven degrees. Terminal velocity: 14.3 kilometers per second. Impact duration: 0.089 seconds.
3669|
3670|"Hold," she said. "Wind's picking up."
3671|
3672|Proxima b's atmosphere was thinner than Earth's, but the temperature differential between the sunward and shadow sides created predictable convection patterns. Her tablet displayed real-time data. Wind speed climbing: fifteen meters per second, gusting to twenty-two.
3673|
3674|"Six minutes," she said. "Then we lift."
3675|
3676|She walked the perimeter, checking anchor points embedded in bedrock. Each one had been tested to three times the expected load. She'd insisted on that. Kenji had argued it was excessive. He'd also been on the engineering team that signed off on the *Santiago's* heat shield modifications — the ones that failed.
3677|
3678|The memorial's design had sparked debate. Some wanted something abstract, symbolic. Maya had presented her proposal: a physical representation of what went wrong, built from the wreckage itself. A reminder that their new world had been purchased with blood.
3679|
3680|---
3681|
3682|She climbed the scaffolding to inspect the capstone one final time. The triangular piece had been machined from the *Santiago's* primary structural ring — one of the few sections recovered intact from the crash site. Three hundred and ten names were etched into its surface.
3683|
3684|She found Rafael Dominguez's name near the apex. Structural engineer, like her. They'd shared night shifts during the deceleration phase. He'd been the one who caught her miscalculation on the heat distribution models for atmospheric entry.
3685|
3686|He'd been asleep in hibernation when the *Santiago* hit.
3687|
3688|"Wind's dropping," Kenji reported. "Eighteen meters per second. Seventeen. Sixteen."
3689|
3690|"Lift," she commanded.
3691|
3692|The crane's motors hummed. The capstone rose smoothly, its polished surface catching the red sunlight and scattering it across the plaza.
3693|
3694|"Forty meters. Beginning horizontal translation."
3695|
3696|The capstone swung out over the memorial's framework. Maya's throat tightened as the names came into view, each one blazing red in Proxima's light.
3697|
3698|A gust hit from the northwest. Wind speed spiked to twenty-one meters per second.
3699|
3700|"Abort!" Maya shouted.
3701|
3702|"Compensating," the operator said. The capstone swayed but held steady.
3703|
3704|The crane's stabilizers were at ninety-six percent capacity. Maya watched the load vectors on her tablet, her breath held. The thermal model showed the gradient stabilizing.
3705|
3706|"Continue," she said.
3707|
3708|The capstone descended toward its mounting points. Maya watched as the massive triangle aligned with the support columns — each movement precise, mechanical, inevitable.
3709|
3710|"Contact," the operator said.
3711|
3712|The mounting crews secured the capstone. Maya descended and walked beneath the completed structure. The angle created a shadow that pointed directly at the crash site. In the settlement's survey maps, they'd preserved the impact crater. Another memorial, unplanned.
3713|
3714|"It's beautiful," Kenji said, materializing beside her.
3715|
3716|Maya stared up at the three hundred and ten names. "It's necessary."
3717|
3718|"Can it be both?"
3719|
3720|She thought about that. The memorial would stand for as long as the colony survived — decades, centuries maybe. Future generations would walk beneath it, read the names, learn what happened.
3721|
3722|She received a ping on her tablet — the xenoarchaeology team had sent a preliminary report. She opened it while Kenji continued talking. The report contained the correlation analysis between the Neptune entity EM patterns and the crystalline structure found at the ruins.
3723|
3724|The entities weren't random. The pulsing crystal at the center of the ruins was a transmitter — a beacon that had been broadcasting for a hundred thousand years. Its signal, traveling at light-speed, had reached the Solar System, where it manifested as the electromagnetic entities that nearly destroyed the Neptune survey fleet. The ghosts beyond Neptune were the broadcast of a dying civilization, reaching out across the void.
3725|
3726|And the fleet had ridden that signal all the way home.
3727|
3728|Maya looked up at the memorial, at the shadow pointing toward the crash site. The *Santiago* had come within sight of the world whose inhabitants had been broadcasting for a thousand centuries. They'd died without knowing what they'd found.
3729|
3730|She walked to the base of the memorial and knelt. With her gloved hand, she traced a crystalline pattern in the Proximan soil — the same mathematical progression she'd seen in the ruins, the same spiraling fractal that matched the entities' EM signature. She carved it into the stone at the memorial's base, next to the names.
3731|
3732|A hundred thousand years ago, someone built a transmitter on this world. Someone sent a message into the dark. Someone watched their civilization end and chose to broadcast their existence across the void.
3733|
3734|Three hundred and ten humans died reaching this world.
3735|
3736|Two civilizations, separated by a hundred millennia, reaching out across the stars.
3737|
3738|"That's beautiful," Kenji said, reading the pattern. "What is it?"
3739|
3740|"Their names," Maya said quietly. "The ones who were here before us. The ones whose signal carried us home."
3741|
3742|---
3743|
3744|That evening, Maya stood alone at the memorial as the settlement's first sunset painted the sky in shades of crimson and amber. The colony's lights were coming online across the valley — habitation modules, greenhouses, the fusion reactor that would power their first decade.
3745|
3746|Three hundred and ten names burned red above her. And at the base of the memorial, carved into Proximan stone, the spiral pattern of a civilization that had reached across a hundred thousand years to say: *We were here.*
3747|
3748|She pulled out her tablet and opened the file marked "Archaeological Survey — Proximan Ruins." There would be questions to answer, messages to decode, a hundred thousand years of lost history to recover.
3749|
3750|Time to get the math right.
3751|
3752|# Chapter 36: Six Names
3753|
3754|![](chapter_images/ch36.png)
3755|
3756|The memorial wall grew one stone at a time.
3757|
3758|Dr. Sarah Okonkwo knelt in Proxima Centauri b's rust-colored soil, her knees pressing into ground that had never felt human weight before this year. The rock in her hand—smooth gray basalt, probably volcanic—felt wrong somehow. Too light in the 0.9g gravity. Too warm from this red dwarf star that hung perpetually at the horizon, neither rising nor setting in their tidally-locked landing zone.
3759|
3760|She carved the first name with a diamond scribe: **Marcus Webb, Chief Engineer, Unity**.
3761|
3762|Her hands shook. Not from the eighteen-month acclimatization period. Not from the muscle atrophy that physical therapy had mostly corrected. From the simple fact that Marcus should be here, doing this work. He'd survived 120 years in hibernation. Survived the brutal deceleration sequence when Unity's light sail had somehow maintained structural integrity despite the mounting g-forces. He'd even survived the landing.
3763|
3764|The infection killed him three weeks after wake-up.
3765|
3766|"Bacterial mutation in storage," she said aloud, though no one was close enough to hear. Talking to herself had become a habit during the long nights under Proxima's unchanging red glow. "We predicted thirty percent hibernation mortality. We didn't predict that our own frozen antibiotics would be the problem."
3767|
3768|She set the stone at the base of the wall and reached for another.
3769|
3770|**Elena Vasquez, Geneticist, New Dawn**.
3771|
3772|Elena had died in her pod, of course. One of the 3,657 hibernation failures across the fleet. Sarah had reviewed the logs obsessively, searching for patterns that weren't there. Random cascade failures, exactly as the mission planners had calculated. Elena's pod had simply been one of the thirty percent.
3773|
3774|The wall stood four meters high already, built by hand because someone—Sarah couldn't remember who—had suggested that automation would feel hollow. Wrong. The survivors needed to *build* this, needed to feel the weight of every stone, every name.
3775|
3776|Twelve thousand colonists had left Earth.
3777|
3778|She carved another name.
3779|
3780|---
3781|
3782|The fabrication dome hummed with activity three kilometers away, but here at the memorial site, Sarah heard only wind. Proxima b's atmosphere was denser than Earth's, the pressure higher, the oxygen content lower but still breathable after genetic therapy. The wind carried unfamiliar scents—sulfur compounds, strange hydrocarbons, the sharp mineral tang of soil that had never known organic decomposition.
3783|
3784|Dr. James Okafor found her as she started the seventeenth stone of the morning.
3785|
3786|"Sarah." His voice was gentle. "Council meeting in an hour."
3787|
3788|"I know."
3789|
3790|"You've been here since dawn. Or what passes for dawn." He gestured at Proxima Centauri, fixed at its eternal twilight angle. "You need to eat something."
3791|
3792|She kept carving. **Thomas Park, Medical Officer, Persistence**.
3793|
3794|"Tom's daughter asked about him yesterday," Sarah said. "She was six when we left Earth. Hibernation paused her aging—she's only twelve now. Biologically. But chronologically she's 126 years old, and she doesn't remember what her father looked like."
3795|
3796|"The video archives—"
3797|
3798|"She doesn't want video. She wants him."
3799|
3800|Okafor crouched beside her, his dark hands resting on his knees. He'd been the mission's deputy commander, second-in-line after Commander Zhang. Zhang had died in the *Phoenix* crash during final approach—310 souls lost when their sail tore and they couldn't complete the deceleration burn. Sarah had watched it happen from Unity's observation deck, had seen the ship tumble into Proxima b's upper atmosphere trailing fire and vaporized metal.
3801|
3802|"We all want things we can't have," Okafor said quietly. "But we have 12,180 living colonists who need us focused on survival, not grief."
3803|
3804|"I can do both."
3805|
3806|"Can you?"
3807|
3808|She set down the diamond scribe. "You're relieving me."
3809|
3810|"I'm suggesting you take a break. There's a difference." He gestured at the wall. "How many names left?"
3811|
3812|Sarah pulled up the count on her wrist display, the holographic numbers glowing faintly in the red light. "Four thousand, two hundred and thirty."
3813|
3814|"At your current pace?"
3815|
3816|"Eighteen months. Give or take."
3817|
3818|"Then pace yourself. This is a marathon, Sarah. Not a sprint."
3819|
3820|She wanted to argue, wanted to explain that every hour she didn't spend carving names felt like betrayal. But exhaustion pressed down on her, heavier than Proxima b's 0.9g. She'd been awake for thirty-seven hours straight.
3821|
3822|"One more," she said. "Then I'll come."
3823|
3824|Okafor nodded and stood, but didn't leave. He waited, watching the red star, while Sarah carved the next name with practiced strokes.
3825|
3826|**Commander Li Zhang, Mission Commander, Phoenix**.
3827|
3828|---
3829|
3830|The council met in what had been Unity's command module, now repurposed as the colony's administrative center. Thirteen people around a salvaged conference table—the surviving senior staff from the three ships that had landed successfully. Unity, New Dawn, and Perseverance. The other ships remained in orbit, slowly being cannibalized for parts and materials. Controlled demolition in space, feeding the colony that grew below.
3831|
3832|Dr. Yuki Tanaka, the colony's new chief engineer, pulled up holographic schematics. "We're three weeks ahead of schedule on the hydroponics domes. Soil amendment is proceeding faster than projected—native bacteria are actually compatible with our crop symbiotes. I don't understand the biochemistry yet, but it works."
3833|
3834|"Population health?" Okafor asked.
3835|
3836|Dr. Reeves, who'd taken over as chief medical officer after Tom's death, shook his head. "Still losing people. Mostly elderly colonists whose bodies can't adapt to the atmospheric differences. We're at 12,164 survivors now. Down sixteen since last week."
3837|
3838|Sixteen more names for the wall.
3839|
3840|"Birth rate?" someone asked.
3841|
3842|"First generation born on Proxima b will arrive in approximately six months," Reeves said. "We have forty-three confirmed pregnancies. All progressing normally so far, though we're watching carefully for developmental issues."
3843|
3844|Sarah felt something unknot in her chest. New life. Children who would never know Earth, never know the blue sky that had haunted her dreams for 120 years. Children who would think red twilight was normal, who would breathe this thick air and call it home.
3845|
3846|"Infrastructure priority?" Okafor looked at Tanaka.
3847|
3848|"Permanent habitats. We can't live in these repurposed modules forever. I've identified three sites with stable bedrock and good access to geothermal energy. We start foundation work next month."
3849|
3850|The meeting continued—water reclamation, mineral surveys, communication relay satellites. The mundane, critical work of building civilization from scratch. Sarah listened, contributed when asked, but part of her mind remained at the memorial wall, counting stones, calculating how many more mornings she'd spend carving names into volcanic rock.
3851|
3852|---
3853|
3854|After the meeting, Sarah didn't return to the wall. Instead, she walked to the observation dome—a clear polymer hemisphere that offered an unobstructed view of Proxima b's alien landscape.
3855|
3856|The red sun painted everything in shades of rust and amber. Mountains in the distance, their peaks sharp and uneroded by the thin winds. A lake three kilometers north, its water tinted copper by dissolved minerals. And beyond all of it, the night side of the planet—a wall of absolute darkness where temperatures dropped to -100°C and the atmosphere condensed into nitrogen snow.

{"content": "3102|# Chapter 29: Building Sanctuary
3103|
3104|![](chapter_images/ch29.png)
3105|
3106|The emergency council meeting had been running for four hours, and Maya Volkov was running on fumes.
3107|
3108|"We're not the ones who spent 120 years sleeping while the rest of us kept the formation," said Commander Park of the orbital station *Verity*. Her image flickered on the main display, degraded by the signal delay between orbit and ground. "Those ships are our only way off this rock if something goes wrong."
3109|
3110|"Something *is* wrong." Maya spread her hands across the salvaged conference table — a sheet of hull plating laid across two structural support beams. The community hall smelled of recycled air, unwashed bodies, and the metallic tang of Proxima b's trace sulfur compounds that no filter could fully remove. "We've got twelve thousand people breathing air that has to be scrubbed through systems designed for three hundred. Every ship in orbit represents life support capacity, power generation, fabrication resources that we *need* on the ground."
3111|
3112|"And every ship we dismantle eliminates our evacuation capability."
3113|
3114|"If the colony fails, there's no one left to evacuate."
3115|
3116|The council chamber fell silent. Twelve representatives — six from the ground, six from orbit — sat across from each other in a room built from the ribs of the *Perseverance*, the first ship to land. Through the transparent polymer ceiling, Proxima Centauri hung motionless at the horizon, a baleful red eye watching humanity's first argument on a new world.
3117|
3118|Mayor Osei, the elected leader of the ground colony, leaned forward. "Commander Park. You have my word — we will preserve one ship. The *Verity* stays operational. But we need the *Fitzgerald*, the *Bolivar*, and the *Nkrumah*. Their hull plating alone can give us another hundred meters of habitable dome space. Their power cores can run the greenhouses for a decade."
3119|
3120|"And what happens when the next flare hits and your domes aren't shielded enough? What happens when you realize Proxima b's radiation environment degrades your equipment three times faster than projections? You'll come back to orbit asking for ships we've already turned into housing."
3121|
3122|"It's a calculated risk."
3123|
3124|"It's a bet with twelve thousand lives."
3125|

3129|
3130|The meeting ended without resolution. Maya stepped outside the hall into Proxima b's perpetual twilight, the planet's eternal sunset painting the colony in shades of rust and shadow. 3133|
3134|"Council still deadlocked?" Tan appeared beside her, his coveralls streaked with regolith dust. He'd been the colony's chief engineer since wake-up, the man who'd designed the retractable radiation shield after the first flare knocked out their greenhouse.
3135|
3136|"Park wants a guarantee we won't touch the *Verity*."
3137|
3138|"Can we give one?"
3139|
3140|Maya shook her head. "Not if we want to expand the habitat to hold twelve thousand permanent residents. The projections are tight. We need those ships."
3141|
3142|Wei followed her gaze to the salvage operation. "The orbitals don't trust us. Can you blame them? They spent 120 years in the dark, awake for six-month stretches, watching ships die. They've seen the math fail too many times."
3143|
3144|"And now they're watching us turn their only escape route into housing."
3145|
3146|"Would you trust us if you were them?"
3147|
3148|Maya had no answer. She watched the plasma torches carve through the landing strut — a ship that had carried people across the gulf between stars, now being reduced to spare parts.

3151|
3152|At midnight, Maya found Commander Park alone on the *Verity's* observation deck. The orbital station rotated slowly, generating artificial gravity that felt almost like Earth. 3153|
3154|"You should be sleeping," Maya said.
3155|
3156|"Shouldn't you?"
3157|
3158|Maya sat in the chair beside Park. The stars beyond Proxima b were unfamiliar — constellations that had never known human names, arranged in patterns no Earthbound astronomer had charted. 3163|
3164|"We dismantle the *Fitzgerald* now — this week. We use her hull to expand the hydroponics domes. Her power core goes to the water extraction plant. In exchange, the *Bolivar* and *Nkrumah* stay in orbit, fully operational, for one year. After that, we reassess."
3165|
3166|"One year."
3167|
3168|"Long enough to prove the colony is viable. Short enough that you can evacuate if it's not."
3169|
3170|Park was silent for a long moment. The station hummed around them — life support cycling, power conduits thrumming, the constant whisper of a machine ecology keeping humans alive in a place that had never known life.

3173|

3175|

3183|

3185|
3186|---
3187|

3189|
3190|The colony was learning. Each failure taught them something. Each compromise gave them another day.
3191|
3192|Maya's tablet buzzed. A message from Park: *Bolivar and Nkrumah are yours. Use them well.*

3195|

3197|
3198|# Chapter 30: The Colony
3199|

3201|

3203|
3204|The planet threw flares at them — three in the first month, one strong enough to knock out surface power for sixty hours. It poisoned their crops. 3257|

3263|

3265|

function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

REPLACE MODE (mode='replace', default): find a unique string and replace it. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, path, old_string, new_string.
PATCH MODE (mode='patch'): apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, patch.

mode.description: Edit mode. 'replace' (default): requires path + old_string + new_string. 'patch': requires patch content only.

path.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. File path to edit.

old_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include surrounding context lines to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Replacement text. Pass empty string '' to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
REQUIRED when mode='patch'. V4A format patch content. Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Almost always pair with notify_on_complete=true — bg without notify runs SILENTLY and you have no way to learn it finished short of calling process(action='poll') yourself. Two legitimate uses:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers, daemons) — silent is correct, there's no exit to notify on.
  (2) Long-running bounded tasks (tests, builds, deploys, CI pollers, batch jobs) — MUST set notify_on_complete=true. Without it you'll either forget to poll or sit blocked waiting for the user to surface the result.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Almost always pair with notify_on_complete=true — without it, the process runs silently and you'll have no way to learn it finished short of calling process(action='poll') yourself (easy to forget, leading to silent blindness on long jobs). Two legitimate patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers, daemons) — these stay silent because there's no exit to notify on. (2) Long-running bounded tasks (tests, builds, deploys, CI pollers, batch jobs) — these MUST set notify_on_complete=true. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.
